models_evaluated: RSNA 2019 second-place open-source ICH model (ResNeXt-101 + BiLSTM)

links.outcome: Whether a monitoring model can detect errors in deployed AI output without ground-truth labels
links.effect: Reviewing decreased-confidence cases gave relative accuracy gains of 4.66, 11.28 and 38.57% vs false-alarm rates of 0.89, 0.45 and 0.14% for ICH-positive predictions at 30, 15 and 5% prevalence.
links.quote: For example, reviewing cases where EMM showed decreased confidence led to substantial relative accuracy gains that outweighed the burden of false alarms.

links.outcome: Accuracy of the primary model stratified by case-level confidence from EMM agreement
links.effect: Accuracy was highest with high EMM agreement and lowest with low agreement, for both ICH-positive and ICH-negative predictions and at all prevalences.
links.quote: As expected, overall accuracy was highest for cases in which the primary model and EMM showed high agreement, and overall accuracy was lowest when EMM showed a lower agreement level with the primary model.

links.outcome: Ability of EMM to flag unreliable predictions from deployed black-box AI, and its failures
links.effect: EMM had 100% agreement with the FDA-cleared model but failed to detect its errors in 138 cases (4%); it was proposed but not tested for longitudinal drift.
links.quote: Finally, in 138 cases (4%, 117 ICH-positive, 21 ICH-negative), EMM demonstrated 100% agreement with the FDA-cleared primary model, but EMM failed to detect that the FDA-cleared primary model’s prediction was wrong.

links.outcome: EMM error-detection performance across gender, age and race subgroups
links.effect: Discrepancies in EMM performance were found in some gender, age and race subgroups, possibly from underrepresentation in the training data or distribution mismatch.
links.quote: Additionally, we analyzed EMM performance across gender, age and race groups and found discrepancies in some subgroups, potentially due to either underrepresentation in the EMM training data or the distribution mismatch between the EMM training data and our internal testing dataset for these subgroups (Supplementary Fig. 6 ).

links.outcome: False confidence when the confidence estimator agrees with an incorrect primary AI prediction
links.effect: EMM showed full agreement with an incorrect primary prediction in 138 cases (4%), mainly subtle hemorrhages or hemorrhage mimics, which could instill false confidence.
links.quote: Of particular concern are instances where EMM fails simultaneously with the primary model while indicating complete consensus, as this could instill false confidence in clinicians and potentially increase misdiagnosis risk.

models_evaluated: FDA-cleared commercial intracranial hemorrhage detection model
open-source RSNA 2019 ICH Detection Challenge second-place model

links.effect: 100% agreement was correct in 1479 cases (51%); high agreement had highest accuracy and lower agreement had lowest accuracy across 30%, 15%, and 5% prevalences.
links.quote: As expected, overall accuracy was highest for cases in which the primary model and EMM showed high agreement, and overall accuracy was lowest when EMM showed a lower agreement level with the primary model.

links.outcome: Low-confidence deferral accuracy and false alarms
links.effect: ICH-positive: +4.66, +11.28, and +38.57% versus false alarms 0.89, 0.45, and 0.14%; ICH-negative net benefit only at 30%.
links.quote: However, this net benefit was only observed for cases with ICH-negative primary model predictions at 30% prevalence (false-alarm rate of 1.05% versus relative accuracy improvement of 3.35%).

links.effect: 100% EMM agreement failed to detect wrong FDA-cleared model predictions in 138 cases (4%; 117 ICH-positive, 21 ICH-negative).
links.quote: Finally, in 138 cases (4%, 117 ICH-positive, 21 ICH-negative), EMM demonstrated 100% agreement with the FDA-cleared primary model, but EMM failed to detect that the FDA-cleared primary model’s prediction was wrong.

links.effect: Discrepancies found across gender, age, and race subgroups; main text reports no subgroup-specific estimates.
links.quote: Additionally, we analyzed EMM performance across gender, age and race groups and found discrepancies in some subgroups, potentially due to either underrepresentation in the EMM training data or the distribution mismatch between the EMM training data and our internal testing dataset for these subgroups (Supplementary Fig. 6 ).

links.outcome: accuracy gains versus false alarm burden from deferral
links.effect: Reviewing low-confidence cases yielded net accuracy gains over false alarms across all prevalences for positive predictions, but for negative predictions net benefit occurred only at 30% prevalence (3.35% gain vs 1.05% false alarms).
links.quote: However, this net benefit was only observed for cases with ICH-negative primary model predictions at 30% prevalence (false-alarm rate of 1.05% versus relative accuracy improvement of 3.35%).
